The Axioms of Creordics

A Thermodynamic Philosophy

Foundational Axioms

Primary Axiom

All complex systems self-organize to access and dissipate energy and information gradients more efficiently than simpler arrangements would allow.

This fundamental principle establishes that complexity emerges not randomly but as a thermodynamic necessity. Systems develop organized structures precisely because these structures enable more effective gradient processing than would be possible through direct, unstructured dissipation.

Axiom of Dissipative Capital Formation

Systems necessarily face continuous trade-offs between immediate gradient dissipation and investment in structures that enhance future dissipative capacity.

Just as organisms allocate energy between immediate needs and growth, all complex systems must balance present performance with capacity building. This axiom recognizes that apparent reductions in immediate dissipation may serve larger thermodynamic imperatives when they build infrastructure for enhanced lifetime gradient processing.

Axiom of Gradient Coupling

When multiple systems share access to common gradients, they become thermodynamically coupled, with coupling strength determined by the intensity of gradient sharing and interdependence of dissipative capacities.

This principle quantifies the connections between systems based on their mutual reliance on shared resources. Strong coupling emerges when systems intensively share gradients or when their dissipative capacities significantly interdepend.

Axiom of Proportional Obligation

Ethical responsibility between systems scales proportionally with the strength of their thermodynamic coupling.

This axiom provides naturalistic grounding for graduated duties, explaining why we bear greater obligations to systems with which we share strong thermodynamic coupling while still acknowledging responsibilities to more distant systems.

Axiom of Information Manifestation

Information gradients influence system organization only through their eventual manifestation as energy gradients via physical processes.

Information affects physical reality exclusively when it triggers energy-dissipating processes. A price differential drives behavior only through energy-consuming transactions; knowledge motivates action only through metabolically expensive neural activity. This grounds information theory in thermodynamic reality.

Axiom of Hierarchical Nesting

Systems exist as components within hierarchically nested structures, where optimization at any single scale that undermines higher-order system capacity violates thermodynamic efficiency.

Every system operates simultaneously as a whole and as a component within larger systems. Actions that maximize performance at one scale while degrading the dissipative capacity of coupled systems at other scales represent thermodynamic failure, regardless of local gains.

Axiom of Temporal Extension

Ethical evaluation of actions must account for effects across relevant timescales, as short-term optimization that depletes long-term capacity represents thermodynamic inefficiency.

Different systems operate on vastly different capital formation timescales. This axiom demands that evaluation horizons match the natural rhythms of the systems involved, recognizing that temporal myopia undermines sustainable gradient dissipation.

Derived Principles

The Gradient Capture Paradox

A system enters a state of gradient capture when it maximizes its local gradient access in ways that reduce total gradient availability across the coupled system hierarchy.

This principle, derived from the Axiom of Hierarchical Nesting, identifies a critical failure mode in complex systems. Examples include monopolistic behavior in markets, resource hoarding in organizations, and cancer in biological systems. The paradox reveals how apparent local success can constitute systemic failure when coupling relationships are ignored.

Application

These axioms form the logical foundation of Creordics, enabling derivation of specific principles for decision-making across scales and domains. By grounding ethical evaluation in measurable physical processes rather than cultural convention, they provide an objective framework for navigating complex trade-offs in interconnected systems.
